title: GLASS mocks, tomographic (preliminary, 65 of 70 seeds)
summary: Each chip asks whether the 65 mock PTEs of one joint B-mode test are uniform, which they are when the analytic covariance describes the scatter of the mocks. It does for Cℓ BB, Cℓ EB and ξ− B (12–83′); for COSEBIs B, ξ+ B (12–83′), ξ± B (12–83′) and ξ± B (2–20′) the mocks scatter 6–9% more than the analytic covariance says (mean χ²/dof 1.06–1.09), so those tests' analytic PTEs read slightly low on the data too. Preliminary: 65 of 70 seeds, the rest arriving today. The mocks are matched to the data cell's bins and n(z). The blinded data's Cℓ BB additive-template amplitude, 0.77 ± 0.22, lies 3.2σ above the mock mean, with 0 of 65 mocks higher; we read this as an additive B-mode systematic in the data, which mocks without systematics do not produce.
banner: GLASS mocks under a throwaway blind; the input cosmology is known. The data B modes shown against them are blinded data, which the blind leaves unchanged
lacks: Sampled mocks have unit weights, Gaussian shape noise at the data's per-bin σ_e and n_eff, no PSF leakage and no additive B mode, so this run has no PSF section.
provenance: GLASS sampled mocks on the v2 tomographic footprint (4,065 deg²), 65 of 70 seeds, nside 4096, each bin's n_eff and σ_e from the data
recalibrated DR6 BPZ+SOM four-bin n(z) and bins of CosmoStat/sp_validation#468, the same as the data cell

headline_note: Covariance checks: KS p-value that the 65 mock PTEs of each joint B-mode test are uniform, as they are when the analytic covariance describes the mock scatter

tables.caption: Each joint B-mode test runs over all ten bin pairs on every mock, against the analytic covariance. A PTE (probability to exceed) is the chance that pure noise gives a χ² at least this large. Mean mock χ²/dof is 1 and the median PTE 0.5 when the analytic covariance describes the mock scatter; about 3.2 mocks per test fall below 0.05 by chance.
Joint B-mode null tests of the blinded data over all ten bin pairs. The rescaled PTE multiplies the analytic covariance by the mocks' mean χ²/dof; the last column counts mocks directly.

columns.label: data PTE, covariance rescaled to the mocks
fraction of 65 mocks with larger χ²

tables.caption: χ² ignores sign; an additive B mode (PSF leakage, a shared shear offset) pushes B modes the same way across scales and pairs. The template amplitude A is the least-squares fit of C_BB = A × 2.6×10⁻¹¹ exp[−(ℓ/2000)²] to Cℓ BB with the analytic covariance; the mean data/σ averages each element over its analytic standard deviation. The mocks have no additive B, so they give each number's null distribution.

figures.caption: Cumulative distribution of the 65 mocks' PTEs for each joint B-mode test, against the uniform distribution (grey diagonal) expected when the analytic covariance is right. A curve above the diagonal means too many low PTEs: the mocks scatter more than the analytic covariance says.
figures.alt: Cumulative distribution of the 65 mocks' PTEs for each joint B-mode test, against the uniform distribution (grey diagonal) expected when the analytic covariance is right. A curve above the diagonal means too many low PTEs: the mocks scatter more than the analytic covariance says.

figures.caption: Variance of the 65 mocks divided by the analytic variance, averaged over each statistic's elements, per bin pair. E rows use ξ± at 12–83′ and Cℓ EE at ℓ 300–1600. With 65 Gaussian mocks a single element's ratio has a 68% range of 0.83–1.17; these averages scatter less.
